newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Western envoys await details on Mostar arrests.
newsitem.headline: Western envoys await details on Mostar arrests.

text.p: The Croatian government has yet to announce any indictments or other details surrounding the reported arrest of Bosnian Croat nationalist mafia chieftains, an international official said on Friday.
Croatian media reported that feared warlords in the Bosnian town of Mostar had been arrested in a crackdown on crime but few details were available.

The office of the international High Representative to Bosnia, Carl Bildt, said it was told the most powerful warlord in western Mostar, Mladen Naletilic and one of his deputies, Vinko Martinovic, were among those arrested in an alleged sweep.

"We have been told by the Croatian authorities at a very senior level to bear with them, that this is an ongoing process, more arrests are sought, more evidence is sought," Colum Murphy, spokesman for the High Representative, told reporters in Sarajevo.

"The exact nature of the charges we don't know but we know all of these people are mafia related and there are a considerable number of charges that can be levelled against the individuals involved," Murphy said.

Naletilic and the paramilitary gangs dominating western Mostar have been blamed by Western envoys for instilling a climate of fear in the divided town to prevent its reunification as required by the Dayton peace agreement.
The Zagreb government has so far failed to uphold previous promises to remove hardliners in Bosnian Croat-held territory, who enjoy strong links to President Franjo Tudjman's ruling party.
There was still no sign that Bosnian Croat authorities had arrested three Croat policemen who were photographed firing on Moslem procession this month in western Mostar, Murphy added.

The deputy police chief, Ivan Hrkac, one of three policemen photographed, had gone missing after international police monitors issued results of their investigation into the shooting incident in Mostar.
"The deputy police chief is missing and is being sought," Murphy said.
At the request of the High Representative, the Canadian government had decided to bar the three policemen from travelling to Canada, Murphy said.
The European Union had yet to address the High Representative's proposal to bar the three men from entering western European countries.

Western and Bosnian government officials, who asked not to be named, said there were reports that Croatia had sent in special forces to Mostar to make the arrests, which would amount to a violation of Bosnia's sovereignty.
But Murphy said Zagreb officials denied the reports.

"The operation took place in association with the Croatian police. But we were assured by the highest level of Croatian authorities that no Croatian police actually carried out arrests on the soil of Bosnia-Herzegovina," he said.
A Bosnian Moslem official, who asked not to be named, said the Croat mafia had turned into a political liability for Tudjman at home and abroad but time would tell if the crackdown was serious.
The official said Zagreb authorities needed to announce charges against Natelicic to dispel speculation that he might be detained only temporarily.
